contrastMetadata.transferBoundary: Threshold objectives can support a monotonic moving boundary under suitable value constraints, while exact-sum objectives often require matching cumulative-state differences; equality wording alone never proves a sliding window.

items.prompt: All values and the target k are positive, and the task asks for the minimum non-empty length with sum at least k. Which objective signal favors a variable window?

options.text: The threshold becomes true monotonically as right expands, and shrinking searches shorter valid intervals.
The answer requires an earlier prefix equal to currentPrefix - k.
The values should be sorted before choosing a range.
Every problem containing a sum uses the same method.

feedback.reason: The inequality and positive values create a validity region that can be repaired and minimized by moving boundaries.

blocks.text: Separate the objective from the data domain

Maintain sum for [left, right]. Adding the next positive value can only increase sum, so expansion is the only move that can turn sum < k into sum >= k. Once the threshold is met, record the current length, remove a[left], and repeat while the interval remains valid; every successful removal produces a shorter candidate ending at the same right. Strict positivity makes removal decrease sum, so after validity is lost no still-shorter interval with that right can recover it. This directional repair is what supports the window; the objective is an inequality region, not a request to match one exact prefix difference.

blocks.title: Name the missing condition
blocks.text: “Contiguous sum” is not an algorithm. First identify whether the result is a threshold, an exact equality, a count, or an optimization; then inspect the signs and whether boundaries are known or must be discovered. A window needs a legal directional update, while prefix state records the boundary history that an equality query may need.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.exact_prefix: Looking specifically for earlierPrefix = currentPrefix - k detects equality. Here every sum greater than k is also valid, and positive boundary effects permit direct minimization.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_values: Sorting changes which values are adjacent, so a range in sorted order is not a subarray of the original sequence.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_sum: The word sum does not supply a movement invariant. The at-least objective and positive values jointly justify this boundary rule.

items.prompt: Values may be negative, and the task asks whether any subarray sums exactly to k. Which signal favors prefix-hash state?

options.text: Exact equality is expressed as currentPrefix - earlierPrefix = k without relying on monotone boundary moves.
Shrink when sum is above k and expand when below k.
Treat all negative values as zero.
Sort values and search adjacent blocks.

feedback.reason: Exact sum is a relation between two cumulative boundaries.

blocks.text: Separate the objective from the data domain

Let P[j] be the sum before index j, with P[0] = 0. A non-empty interval [i, j - 1] sums to k exactly when P[j] - P[i] = k, or P[i] = P[j] - k. Scan boundaries from left to right while storing prior prefix values in a hash set initialized with 0. At boundary j, compute P[j] and test whether P[j] - k has appeared before; query before inserting the current boundary so a zero target cannot manufacture an empty interval. This algebra is independent of signs. Negative values break sum-based expand/shrink direction but do not change prefix subtraction.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.threshold_window: With mixed signs, adding a value can decrease the sum and removing one can increase it, so above/below k does not identify a safe boundary move.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.positive_assumption: Replacing negative values with zero changes every interval containing them and therefore solves a different input.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_then_scan: Sorting preserves a multiset but destroys original adjacency, so its adjacent blocks do not represent the required subarrays.

items.prompt: All values and k are nonnegative, and the task asks whether a non-empty interval has sum exactly k. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: A carefully defined window can work, while prefix methods also remain correct; workload and edge cases decide.
Exact equality always excludes sliding window.
The same window is correct for arbitrary signed values.
Exact equality cannot be solved on contiguous ranges.

feedback.reason: The words exact sum do not uniquely determine a strategy.

blocks.text: Separate the objective from the data domain

For one scan, add a[right], then remove values from the left only while sum > k. Nonnegative values guarantee that expansion never decreases sum and shrinking never increases it, so a sum above k cannot return to k by expanding and must be repaired from the left. After repair, report success only when sum == k and left <= right; that non-empty check matters when k = 0 and shrinking a positive singleton leaves an empty zero-sum state. A prefix set using P[j] - k is also correct and generalizes to signed values, while a reusable prefix array may fit fixed-boundary queries. Thus equality alone does not select one method.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.prefix_only: Prefix state is valid, but nonnegative boundary effects also support a carefully defined one-pass equality window.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.window_any_sign: A negative entrant or outgoing value can reverse the assumed sum change, so the same discard rule is not safe for arbitrary signs.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.no_method: Both the monotone window under this domain and the prefix-difference identity can detect a contiguous exact sum.

items.prompt: For nonnegative values and a nonnegative budget, a non-empty window has just been shrunk until its sum is at most the budget. Why should its current length be evaluated before right advances?

options.text: After shrinking any over-budget interval, record the current valid length.
Record only when sum equals budget.
Return the first valid interval.
Look only for prefix difference exactly equal to budget.

feedback.reason: The objective accepts every sum below or equal to the budget.

blocks.text: Separate the objective from the data domain

After adding a[right], repeatedly remove a[left] only while sum exceeds the budget. Nonnegative values make every removal non-increasing, so this loop restores validity. When it stops, the current left is the earliest valid start for this right: if a start was just discarded, the interval beginning there was still over budget; if none was discarded, index 0 is already earliest. Therefore right - left + 1 is the longest valid interval ending at right and must be compared with the global maximum before right changes. Equality is not required because every sum below the budget satisfies the at-most contract.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.record_only_equal: The optimal interval may have sum strictly below the budget, so equality would discard valid candidates.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.stop_first: The repaired interval is best only among intervals ending at this right; a later endpoint can produce a longer valid range.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.prefix_match: Searching only for prefix difference equal to the budget ignores every interval whose smaller sum is still valid.

items.prompt: A static array receives many queries for the exact sum of a specified interval [l, r]. Which method is natural?

options.text: Use a prefix difference for the already specified boundaries.
Move boundaries until the sum happens to equal the query answer.
Use a frequency map to discover an unknown start.
Sort each interval before summing.

feedback.reason: Exact can describe either a target value or the arithmetic value of a known interval.

blocks.text: Separate the objective from the data domain

Build P[0] = 0 and P[i + 1] = P[i] + a[i] once for the immutable array. For every inclusive query [l, r], P[r + 1] - P[l] cancels exactly the contribution before l and leaves the arithmetic sum of the already specified interval. Construction costs O(n) and each later query costs O(1). No search is taking place: the query owns both boundaries and asks for their sum, not for an unknown interval whose aggregate equals a target. That distinction makes a prefix array, rather than a moving search window or a prefix-frequency map, the natural reusable representation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.search_window: Moving boundaries would search candidates the query did not ask for; l and r already identify the only interval to evaluate.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.prefix_hash: A hash lookup is useful when an earlier boundary must be discovered from a target difference. Here direct indexed prefix reads already identify both boundaries.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort: Addition is order-independent, so sorting provides no arithmetic benefit; it also breaks the meaning of the original l and r indices.

items.prompt: Values may be negative, and the task asks for the shortest interval with sum at least k. What is the safe conclusion?

options.text: The simple threshold window is invalid; prefix sums with an order-aware structure may be required.
A frequency map for prefix - k always gives the shortest at-least interval.
Use the positive-value shrink rule unchanged.
Sort and use two pointers.

feedback.reason: Threshold versus exact is only one axis; sign constraints are another.

blocks.text: Separate the objective from the data domain

Define P[j] as the sum before index j. The interval [i, j - 1] meets the threshold when P[j] - P[i] >= k, and its length is j - i. A monotonic deque stores candidate earlier indices with increasing prefix values. For each current j, repeatedly use and remove a front while the inequality holds, recording j - front; a later right boundary can only make that same start longer. Then remove back indices whose prefix is at least P[j], because the newer j is both later and no harder to satisfy from in the future, so it dominates them. This ordered prefix state handles signed values without assuming local sum direction.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.positive_window: A negative entrant can lower the sum and removing a negative value can raise it, so the positive-domain expand/shrink repair discards starts without proof.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_values: Sorting changes original adjacency, so two nearby sorted values need not form any interval in the input.

items.prompt: Which phrase most directly changes an exact-sum problem into a threshold problem?

options.text: "sum at least k" instead of "sum exactly k."
Adding the word contiguous.
Calling the sequence an array.
Using the word target.

feedback.reason: Equality selects one aggregate value; a threshold selects a range of valid values.

blocks.text: Separate the objective from the data domain

“Exactly k” accepts only aggregate k; “at least k” accepts the entire region [k, infinity). For example, a one-element sum of 7 is valid for an at-least-5 objective but invalid for an exact-5 objective. Under positive values, this semantic change also alters timing: a minimum-at-least window records every valid interval before shrinking further, whereas an exact-sum window records only equality and treats a larger sum as a state to repair. The phrase changes the result contract, but it still does not prove a simple window is legal; arbitrary signed values can remove the directional boundary effect.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target: A target can be used by equality, at-least, or at-most predicates; the comparison operator supplies the semantics.

items.prompt: The result asks for how many subarrays sum exactly to k. Why is a minimum-length threshold window the wrong abstraction?

options.text: Counting every exact match requires preserving all matching start boundaries, not only one current valid window.
Counts cannot refer to contiguous intervals.
A window cannot maintain a sum.
Prefix values must be sorted first.

feedback.reason: The result contract requires multiplicity of exact cumulative differences.

blocks.text: Separate the objective from the data domain

With P[0] = 0, every earlier boundary i satisfying P[i] = P[j] - k creates a distinct exact-sum interval ending before j. Store a frequency for each prefix value. At current boundary j, add frequency[P[j] - k] to the answer, then increment frequency[P[j]]; querying first excludes an empty interval when k = 0. Equal prefix values can occur at several indices, especially with zeros or signed cancellation, and every occurrence must contribute separately. A minimum-threshold window keeps only one evolving left boundary and one best length, so it deliberately discards precisely the multiplicity the count contract requires.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.window_no_sum: A window can maintain one sum, but one sum and one left boundary do not retain every earlier prefix occurrence that forms a distinct match.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.prefix_sorted: Sorting prefix values would lose their scan-time boundary relation. Hash frequencies count matching prior values online in original order.

items.prompt: All values and the target k are positive. The task asks for the maximum length with sum exactly k. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: A monotone window can search equality, but zeros are absent and answer timing must retain the longest matching state.
Exact equality is identical to sum at most k.
Prefix differences cannot represent exact sums.
An exact-sum window requires negative values.

feedback.reason: Strict positivity creates monotone sum movement even for an equality objective.

blocks.text: Separate the objective from the data domain

Add a[right] to the current sum. While sum > k, remove a[left] and advance left; strict positivity proves that expansion would only increase an already excessive sum and that each removal decreases it. When the repaired sum equals k, compare right - left + 1 with the longest answer. Do not record sum < k, because that interval satisfies an at-most predicate but not equality, and do not shrink an equal positive interval before recording it because removing anything makes it too small. Prefix differences also remain correct; storing the earliest index for each needed prefix yields the longest exact interval and generalizes beyond positive values.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.threshold_same: An interval with sum below k is valid for at-most but invalid for exact equality, so the two result sets and optima can differ.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.prefix_invalid: For any signs, P[r + 1] - P[l] is the interval sum; equality is exactly the relation that prefix lookup expresses.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.negative_required: Strict positivity supplies the monotone movement used here. Negative values remove that simple-window guarantee rather than enabling it.

options.text: Choose sliding window whenever the prompt mentions a contiguous sum.
For a threshold, check whether value signs create monotone boundary effects.
For exact sums with arbitrary signs, consider historical prefix lookup.
For many fixed-boundary queries, consider precomputed prefix differences.

feedback.reason: The same surface words cover several different search and query contracts.

blocks.text: Separate the objective from the data domain

“Contiguous sum” identifies only the candidate shape. A minimum or maximum threshold may support a moving validity boundary when signs make addition and removal directional. Exact sum under arbitrary signs instead becomes the historical relation P[i] = P[j] - k. If l and r are already supplied for many immutable queries, no boundary search is needed and a prefix array answers by subtraction. The same surface phrase therefore maps to different legal state depending on objective, value domain, who chooses boundaries, and whether preprocessing is reused. Choosing a window before checking those facts is the invalid rule.

items.prompt: Which facts support a threshold sliding window? Select all that apply.

options.text: The answer uses at-least or at-most validity rather than one exact value.
Value constraints make expansion and shrinking directional.
The scan can maintain one current candidate interval.
Values are arbitrary signed with no stronger invariant.

feedback.reason: Threshold wording is useful only together with a monotone value domain and matching boundary search.

blocks.text: Separate the objective from the data domain

These facts work as a bundle. An inequality defines a validity region rather than one aggregate value. A constrained value domain must then make boundary effects directional: for nonnegative sums, expansion cannot decrease the aggregate and shrinking cannot increase it. Finally, the workload must be expressible as one interval whose boundaries advance without needing discarded starts later. Under those conditions an at-most window can shrink after violation, while a minimum-at-least window can record and shrink while valid. Arbitrary signed values remove the movement proof; a negative entrant can lower a sum and removing a negative can raise it, so threshold wording alone is not enough.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.arbitrary_negatives: Without a stronger invariant, signed values make both expansion and shrinking capable of moving the sum in either direction, so the simple window cannot prove a discarded start is useless.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.inequality: At-least or at-most semantics create a region that can remain valid across several sums and be repaired after crossing its boundary.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.monotone_values: Directional aggregate changes are the proof that a specific expand or shrink move cannot skip a better candidate.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.one_evolving_interval: A simple window retains one candidate; it fits only when earlier discarded boundaries are not needed for later outputs.

items.prompt: Which facts support exact-sum prefix state? Select all that apply.

options.text: A valid interval satisfies currentPrefix - earlierPrefix = k.
Values may be positive, zero, or negative.
Counting or optimizing may require information about several earlier boundaries.
Only the first threshold-valid interval matters.

feedback.reason: Prefix state retains historical boundary information for exact equality.

blocks.text: Separate the objective from the data domain

For prefix boundaries P[i] and P[j], interval [i, j - 1] sums exactly to k when P[j] - P[i] = k, so the lookup key at j is P[j] - k. This identity remains true for positive, zero, and negative values because it is algebra, not a movement rule. What the hash map stores depends on the result: a set for existence, frequency for count, earliest index for longest length, or latest useful index for shortest length. Several earlier boundaries can share a value and represent distinct candidates. A “first threshold-valid interval” neither tests equality nor preserves the payload required by these contracts.

items.prompt: Which tasks can admit either a window or prefix method under nonnegative values? Select all that apply.

options.text: Existence of an exact-sum interval.
All length-k interval sums.
Maximum length-k sum.
Shortest sum-at-least interval using only the ordinary shrink rule with arbitrary negatives.

feedback.reason: Some contracts leave both strategies legal.

blocks.text: Separate the objective from the data domain

For nonnegative exact-sum existence, a monotone equality window can shrink only while sum > k, while a prefix set can look for P[j] - k; both are correct, with different generality and state. For all fixed-size sums, a rolling sum transfers adjacent blocks in O(1) per shift and a prefix array subtracts any requested pair of boundaries. The maximum fixed-size sum can reduce the outputs from either enumeration. These are legal alternatives, so access pattern, reuse, and memory decide. The ordinary shrink rule does not become legal for arbitrary signed shortest-at-least merely because a stronger prefix/deque solution exists.

items.prompt: Which edge cases clarify the threshold-versus-exact boundary? Select all that apply.

options.text: Zeros that create several windows with the same sum.
Intervals exceed k but none equal k.
Several exact matches with different lengths.
Only one case where exact and threshold happen to return the same interval.

feedback.reason: Good tests separate the accepted aggregate set and the output objective.

blocks.text: Separate the objective from the data domain

Use tests that force the contracts apart. With [0, 0] and k = 0, several non-empty exact intervals share the same sum, exposing whether the output is existence, count, shortest, or longest and whether empty state is excluded. With [3] and k = 2, an at-least interval exists but no exact interval does. With [1, 0] and k = 1, exact matches of lengths one and two show that equality still needs an optimization payload. A case containing only one interval that happens to satisfy both equality and a threshold cannot reveal any of these differences and may let the wrong algorithm appear correct.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.only_one_hit: When both contracts coincidentally return the same sole interval, the test cannot expose incorrect acceptance of larger sums, lost multiplicity, or wrong length optimization.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.zeros: Repeated equal prefixes create multiple exact starts and make empty-versus-non-empty and update timing observable.

items.prompt: Which mistaken claims collapse threshold and exact-sum objectives into one rule? Select all that apply.

options.text: Exact sum can never use a sliding window.
Every threshold objective supports a simple window.
Contiguity alone decides between the methods.
Exact subarray sum is a prefix difference.

feedback.reason: Objective labels must be combined with value and workload constraints.

blocks.text: Separate the objective from the data domain

Each selected claim promotes one surface feature into a universal method and is false. Exact equality can use a window when nonnegative values make above-target repair monotone. A threshold can reject a simple window when arbitrary signs destroy that same repair proof. Contiguity is shared by moving windows, prefix differences, and stronger prefix structures, so it cannot choose among them. By contrast, P[r + 1] - P[l] equals the sum of [l, r] for any numeric signs; this is a valid algebraic identity. The identity may motivate prefix state, but strategy still depends on the output payload and workload.

items.prompt: Compare two legal O(n) strategies: a nonnegative threshold window storing only sum and boundaries, and an arbitrary-signed exact-sum prefix-hash scan.
constraints: The prefix hash may retain n distinct prefix values.

feedback.reason: Both can be linear under their respective contracts, but they solve different objective and value-domain problems.

blocks.text: Separate the objective from the data domain

For the nonnegative threshold window, right advances through n positions once and left also advances at most n times; nested syntax therefore performs at most 2n boundary moves, giving O(n) time. The prompt limits its state to a sum and two boundaries, so auxiliary space is O(1). The exact-sum path computes one prefix per value and performs a constant expected-time hash lookup and update at each of n boundaries, giving expected O(n) time. Up to n distinct historical prefix values and their payloads may remain live, so auxiliary space is O(n). The equal time bounds do not make the strategies interchangeable: the hash spends history to avoid the window's monotone-domain requirement.

blocks.title: Name the missing condition
blocks.text: “Contiguous sum” is not an algorithm. First identify whether the result is a threshold, an exact equality, a count, or an optimization; then inspect the signs and whether boundaries are known or must be discovered. A window needs a legal directional update, while prefix state records the boundary history that an equality query may need.

contrastSets.transferBoundary: Threshold objectives can support a monotonic moving boundary under suitable value constraints, while exact-sum objectives often require matching cumulative-state differences; equality wording alone never proves a sliding window.
